youtube.title: Why Did Myspace Die? Worth $580 Million, Sold for $35 Million
youtube.description:
Why did Myspace die? In July 2006 it was the most visited website in the United States, ahead of Google, and News Corp had bought its parent for $580 million. Six years later, Myspace sold for a reported $35 million. This is the story of what happened to Myspace, from a giant Google ad guarantee tied to traffic targets to the crowd moving to Facebook. It asks why Myspace failed just as a plainer rival opened its doors to everyone.

This documentary follows the deal at the centre of the story: a giant advertising guarantee tied to traffic targets, signed just as a plainer rival opened its doors to everyone. It covers how the pages filled with ads, how the crowd moved to Facebook, the chief executives and the two rounds of layoffs, the sale, and the 50 million songs lost years later. Every figure is sourced.

{CHAPTERS}

Sources
- News Corporation press release, 18 July 2005
- Derived from the News Corporation press release, 18 July 2005, and the sale reports of 29 June 2011 below

- News Corporation and Google joint announcement, 7 August 2006
- Derived: $900 million minimum over about three and a half years (joint announcement, 7 August 2006) against the $580 million price (press release, 18 July 2005); payments depended on the traffic commitments
- H.R. 5319, Deleting Online Predators Act, House vote of 26 July 2006; not passed by the Senate in the 109th Congress
- Joint statement of MySpace and the state attorneys general, 14 January 2008
- David Kirkpatrick, The Facebook Effect (Simon & Schuster, 2010)
- Facebook announcement, 26 September 2006
- Facebook Platform announcement, f8 event, 24 May 2007
- Microsoft press release, 24 October 2007
- Derived: $15 billion (Microsoft, 24 October 2007) divided by $580 million (News Corporation, 18 July 2005) is about 25.9
- Google fourth-quarter 2007 earnings call, 31 January 2008
- comScore worldwide data, reported June 2008
- Facebook blog post, 8 April 2009
- News Corporation announcement, 22 April 2009
- comScore US data for May 2009, reported June 2009
- Myspace announcement, 16 June 2009
- News Corporation announcement, 10 February 2010
- Myspace relaunch announcement, 27 October 2010
- Myspace announcement, 11 January 2011
- News Corporation earnings call, 2 February 2011
- Derived: Hitwise ranking, July 2006 (Reuters, 11 July 2006), to News Corporation earnings call, 2 February 2011
- News Corporation announcement, 29 June 2011; price as reported by The Wall Street Journal and AllThingsD, 29 June 2011
- Specific Media announcement, 29 June 2011
- Derived: reported $35 million (29 June 2011) divided by $580 million (18 July 2005) is about 0.06
- Facebook IPO pricing, 17 May 2012
- Time Inc announcement, 11 February 2016
- The Guardian, 18 March 2019
- Estimate by technologist Andy Baio, reported in The Guardian, 18 March 2019
- Microsoft offer letter, 1 February 2008; Yahoo board rejection, 11 February 2008

How this was made: an original script, researched and fact-checked from the sources above. Maps, charts and graphics are our own; some footage is licensed stock, and scenes no camera filmed are illustrations made with AI tools. The narration is a synthetic voice.

sources.claim: In July 2005 News Corp agreed to buy Intermix Media, Myspace's parent, for $12 a share in cash, about $580 million
Six years later News Corp sold Myspace for a reported $35 million (2005 purchase to 2011 sale)
sources.source: Derived from the News Corporation press release, 18 July 2005, and the sale reports of 29 June 2011 below

sources.claim: Myspace was launched in August 2003 inside the Los Angeles internet company eUniverse, later renamed Intermix
Myspace was modelled on Friendster, an older social site struggling to keep up with its own growth
Every new member had cofounder Tom Anderson added as a friend by default
In September 2005 News Corp agreed to buy IGN Entertainment for $650 million, and grouped its internet properties in Fox Interactive Media
Myspace registered its 100 millionth account in August 2006
sources.source: CNET, 9 August 2006, reporting the company's announcement

sources.claim: In July 2006 Hitwise counted Myspace as the most visited website in the US, with 4.46 percent of US web visits in one week, ahead of Yahoo Mail, Yahoo's home page and Google
sources.source: Reuters, 11 July 2006, citing Hitwise data for the week ending 8 July 2006

sources.claim: On 7 August 2006 Google became the exclusive search and keyword-targeted advertising provider for Fox Interactive Media sites including Myspace
sources.source: News Corporation and Google joint announcement, 7 August 2006

sources.claim: Google guaranteed minimum revenue-share payments of $900 million, over about three and a half years
sources.source: News Corporation and Google joint announcement, 7 August 2006

sources.claim: The payments were based on Fox Interactive Media achieving certain traffic and other commitments
sources.source: News Corporation and Google joint announcement, 7 August 2006

sources.claim: The guarantee could repay the $580 million purchase within a few years
sources.source: Derived: $900 million minimum over about three and a half years (joint announcement, 7 August 2006) against the $580 million price (press release, 18 July 2005); payments depended on the traffic commitments

sources.claim: Traffic meant page views, executives were under pressure to raise traffic and revenue numbers, and the pages grew busier with ads
Spam accounts and fake profiles spread, and parents and lawmakers raised concerns about children's safety on the site
In July 2006 the US House voted 410 to 15 for a bill requiring schools and libraries to block social networking sites; it never became law
sources.source: H.R. 5319, Deleting Online Predators Act, House vote of 26 July 2006; not passed by the Senate in the 109th Congress

sources.claim: In January 2008 Myspace agreed new child-safety principles with 49 state attorneys general
sources.source: Joint statement of MySpace and the state attorneys general, 14 January 2008

sources.claim: Facebook began at Harvard in February 2004, spread to other colleges, and opened to high schools in 2005
sources.source: David Kirkpatrick, The Facebook Effect (Simon & Schuster, 2010)

sources.claim: Facebook opened to anyone aged 13 or over with an email address on 26 September 2006
In May 2007 Facebook opened its site to outside developers to build apps inside it
sources.source: Facebook Platform announcement, f8 event, 24 May 2007

sources.claim: Microsoft invested $240 million in Facebook at a $15 billion valuation in October 2007
About twenty-six times what News Corp paid for Myspace's parent
sources.source: Derived: $15 billion (Microsoft, 24 October 2007) divided by $580 million (News Corporation, 18 July 2005) is about 25.9

sources.claim: In January 2008 Google cofounder Sergey Brin told investors that advertising on social networks had not worked out as well as Google had hoped
comScore measured Facebook passing Myspace in worldwide monthly unique visitors in April 2008
Facebook announced 200 million active users in April 2009
In April 2009 Chris DeWolfe was replaced as Myspace CEO by former Facebook COO Owen Van Natta; Tom Anderson moved to an adviser role
comScore had Facebook level with Myspace in US unique visitors by May 2009
sources.source: comScore US data for May 2009, reported June 2009

sources.claim: In June 2009 Myspace cut about 30 percent of its staff, roughly 420 jobs
Van Natta left Myspace in February 2010, less than a year after taking over; Mike Jones and Jason Hirschhorn became co-presidents
In October 2010 Myspace relaunched as a social entertainment site focused on music, video and games, with a new logo
In January 2011 Myspace cut 47 percent of its staff, about 500 jobs
In February 2011 News Corp said it was exploring options for Myspace, including a sale
About four and a half years from most visited US site to a company looking for a buyer
sources.source: Derived: Hitwise ranking, July 2006 (Reuters, 11 July 2006), to News Corporation earnings call, 2 February 2011

sources.claim: On 29 June 2011 News Corp sold Myspace to Specific Media, keeping a minority stake; the price was not disclosed and was reported at about $35 million
sources.source: News Corporation announcement, 29 June 2011; price as reported by The Wall Street Journal and AllThingsD, 29 June 2011

sources.claim: Specific Media was run by brothers Tim and Chris Vanderhook, and Justin Timberlake took an ownership stake in the new Myspace
Roughly six cents back on every dollar
sources.source: Derived: reported $35 million (29 June 2011) divided by $580 million (18 July 2005) is about 0.06

sources.claim: Facebook went public in May 2012 at a valuation of about $104 billion
In 2016 Time Inc bought Viant, Myspace's parent, citing its advertising technology and data
In 2019 Myspace said music uploaded more than three years earlier, from about 2003 to 2015, may have been lost in a server migration
The loss was estimated at about 50 million songs from 14 million artists
sources.source: Estimate by technologist Andy Baio, reported in The Guardian, 18 March 2019

sources.claim: Yahoo turned down a $44.6 billion offer from Microsoft in 2008
sources.source: Microsoft offer letter, 1 February 2008; Yahoo board rejection, 11 February 2008
